newsitem.title: CONGO: Rwandan refugees reach Congo after Zaire trek.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees reach Congo after Zaire trek.

text.p: About 3,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have crossed into northern Congo after trekking across Zaire to flee advancing rebels, humanitarian sources said on Monday.
Much larger groups of refugees, estimated by some sources to total up to 40,000, are around the Zairean city of Mbandaka hoping to cross the river separating the two countries by canoe.
The refugees include soldiers of Rwanda's defeated former government army, the FAR, but those who reached Congolese territory in the past few days appeared to have been disarmed, the sources said.

Congolese government officials were not immediately available to comment. State television's news bulletin on Monday night said only "the presence of about 2,000 Hutu refugees has been observed at Liranga".
The rebels are close to Mbandaka but have not yet entered the city where little resistance by government troops was expected, military sources said.
Other Hutus have headed north to Central African Republic and south to Angola and some have crossed the borders.

The 3,000 already inside Congo are around Liranga, some 400 km (250 miles) north-east of the capital Brazzaville. Aid agencies have begun flying the first relief supplies to the isolated area, which has virtually no roads.
The Hutus have walked some 1,600 km (1,000 miles) westward since Laurent Kabila's rebellion began last October and his Tutsi-led fighters drove the refugees out of their camps in eastern Zaire.

The ones reaching Congo are the desperate and exhausted rump of up two million Hutus who fled to eastern Zaire in July 1994, after they were defeated in Rwanda's civil war by Tutsi-led rebels now in power.
Many of the refugees, chiefly the ex-FAR and members of the former Interahamwe militia, committed the 1994 genocide of about 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda.
Thousands of refugees have died of famine and disease during their extraordinary ordeal. Others have been killed by Tutsis among Kabila's rebels, U.N. and other human rights workers say.
Many gave up the fight and are being airlifted from rebel- held Kisangani back to Rwanda where some face arrest for their alleged role in the genocide.
